lesson_title: Dough, Rusks and Broken Paving: How Mountains Happen
hook_text: Every fault landform on earth is lying in your driveway right now.
clip_script: Go out to a cracked concrete path, because every fault landform is lying there in miniature. Two slabs, and one has settled lower than its neighbour — the classic trip hazard. That is a normal fault, and scaled up it prints a fault scarp on the landscape: a step so straight and so long that no river could have made it. Where tree roots have jacked one slab up over the edge of the next, you have a reverse fault — one block forced up and over its neighbour. Now use three slabs. Let the middle one sink between its two neighbours and you are looking down into a rift valley: a flat dropped floor with a straight wall on each side. At full scale that is the East African Rift — a floor wide enough for farms and lakes, walled by scarps hundreds of metres high. Let the middle slab stand proud instead, and you have a block mountain: steep straight sides, flat top, the shape of a table. Folded country rolls in curves; faulted country is drawn with a ruler. Curves mean the rock bent. Straight lines mean it broke.
visual_style: A cracked driveway shot from above, slabs sliding and sinking, then each miniature morphing into its full-scale landform — scarp, rift valley, block mountain — with clean label overlays.
mood: Backyard geology — the whole syllabus hiding at your gate.
pacing: Playful through the slab moves, widening in scale with each morph, crisp landing on 'curves bent, straight broke'.
